title: Salting and Desalting
explain: Salting fixes a hot key: when one key gets more traffic than one partition can take, you write it under several artificial keys so the load spreads, then merge the pieces back when you need the real value. It is divide and conquer in two layers: a first layer scatters, a second layer gathers.
model:
My framing: two processors.

- **Layer 1 (salt):** each incoming event for the hot key gets a random suffix, `item_123` becomes `item_123_0 … item_123_{S-1}`. The key's traffic now lands on up to *S* partitions, and each computes a partial aggregate.
- **Layer 2 (desalt and aggregate):** strip the salt and merge the partials for `item_123` into the final value.

```
events(item_123) ─salt─▶ item_123_k ─partial agg per k─▶ strip salt ─▶ merge ─▶ item_123
```

Rules of thumb:

- Choose `S ≥ hot-key rate / capacity of one partition`, with headroom.
- Salt only the hot keys if you can identify them; the long tail stays one lookup.
- It needs **mergeable** partials: sum, count, min/max, set union, HyperLogLog. Not exact medians or averages of averages.
- You trade read cost for write throughput: a read becomes a scatter-gather over *S* keys.

It is the standard answer to the skew that [sharding](#/sd/f/sharding) produces. Compare with adaptively splitting the range ([token rebalancing](#/sd/f/token-rebalancing)).

details.q: How do you pick the number of salts?
details.a: From load: one item at 90,000 writes/s with a partition safe at 10,000 writes/s needs at least 9 salts; with headroom (target half of capacity, 5,000 per salted key) it is 90,000 / 5,000 = 18.

details.q: Which aggregates can the desalting step compute from the partials?
details.a: Anything with a merge function: sums, counts, min, max, set union, HyperLogLog, top-k sketches. Exact medians, percentiles and an average of per-salt averages cannot be merged; carry (sum, count) instead of the average.
Reads become scatter-gather over S keys, so you spend read cost for write throughput. You also lose single-key atomicity and a simple point lookup.

details.q: Chat messages are salted randomly per conversation and now appear out of order. Why?
details.a: Random salt scatters one conversation across partitions with no shared ordering. Use a deterministic salt (such as `hash(sender_id) % S`) or sequence numbers, so entities that need order stay together.

details.q: A catalog has 10 million items but only 12 are hot. How do you salt?
details.a: Salt just the 12 (detected from metrics or a heavy-hitter sketch) and keep a small registry of which keys are salted. The other 9,999,988 items stay unsalted and keep single-lookup reads.

details.q: Isn't this just sharding the key further?
details.a: Yes: salt is an extra shard-key component for a key that one shard cannot carry. The difference is that you must remember to undo it when reading.

prompts.q: Explain salting and desalting to an interviewer in about 30 seconds, including its cost.
points: Layer 1 appends a random salt to spread writes
Layer 2 strips the salt and merges partials
Cost: reads become scatter-gather over S keys

prompts.q: Design view counting for a viral video that gets 90,000 events/s on one key.
points: Compute S from rate / partition capacity with headroom
Salt writes, partial count per salted key
Periodic merge to the real count
Reads sum S keys or read the merged value

prompts.q: When is random salting the wrong tool, and what do you use instead?
points: Deterministic salt keeps related events together
Alternative: split the hot range adaptively, or cache / replicate the hot key
